summary: This informational memo describes problems of using Mobile IPv4 in networks that connect to the Internet through a VPN gateway, since they lack well-described solutions. It illustrates the problems and proposes guidelines for possible solutions.

eli5.summary: Using a travelling address through a company's secure gate causes trouble. This document explains what goes wrong and what answers should be like.

questions: why does mobile ip fail through vpn gateways
why does mobile ip not work through vpn gateways
what is a foreign agent in mobile ip
how to support roaming mobile users
subtitle: Why Mobile IPv4 breaks when used inside a corporate VPN

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 and IPsec VPN gateways were designed independently, and when a roaming employee tries to use both simultaneously—to stay connected while moving between networks and securely access the corporate intranet—they encounter fundamental incompatibilities that block registration or require repeated tunnel renegotiation.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies five deployment scenarios, analyzes the specific problems in the most common case (Home Agent inside the intranet behind a VPN gateway), and proposes solution guidelines that respect existing VPN infrastructure, IPsec standards, and MIPv4 protocol requirements.
tldr.outcome: The document establishes the requirements for a solution but does not provide the implementation; subsequent RFCs would address solutions like NAT traversal and alternative tunnel orderings.

today: RFC 4093 is Informational and identifies a real problem that persists in networks using both MIPv4 and IPsec VPN. The document itself does not specify a solution, but establishes the requirements that solutions (in subsequent RFCs and vendor implementations) must meet. It remains relevant for understanding why certain MIPv4-VPN coexistence approaches are preferred.

sections.title: The Collision of Two Technologies
sections.content:
Mobile IP version 4 (MIPv4) lets a device keep its home network address and maintain transport connections even when the device moves between networks. IPsec VPN gateways protect corporate intranets by allowing only encrypted, authenticated traffic from remote users. For a corporate employee roaming outside the intranet with a laptop, the ideal outcome is to use both: MIPv4 for continuous mobility and VPN for security.

The problem is that MIPv4 and VPN were designed in isolation. MIPv4 standards assume direct communication with home agents. VPN gateways assume all protected traffic comes through the encrypted tunnel. When an MIPv4 home agent sits behind a VPN gateway, mobile nodes trying to register with the home agent must establish an IPsec tunnel first, forcing MIPv4 traffic to run encrypted inside the VPN. This breaks fundamental assumptions in both protocols.
sections.eli5: Mobile IP helps your laptop stay connected when you move. VPN hides and protects your connection to the office. But if the office uses both, they fight each other because each one expects to control how your packets flow.

sections.title: Five Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The document defines five scenarios based on where the MIPv4 Home Agent (HA) and VPN gateway are located. Scenario 1 places the HA inside the intranet, protected by the VPN gateway—the most common case. The mobile node must first establish an IPsec tunnel to the gateway to reach the HA.

Scenarios 2 and 4 place the HA on the VPN domain border (in the DMZ) or outside entirely. Scenarios 3 and 5 combine the VPN gateway and HA on the same machine or local link. The authors analyze each and determine that Scenario 1 is the most important and practical. If that scenario is solved, the solutions apply to Scenarios 2 and 4 as well. Scenarios 3 and 5 work without special solutions because the gateway and HA are co-located or nearby.
sections.eli5: The home agent can be inside the office, on the border between office and internet, or outside in the operator's network. The closer it is to the VPN gateway, the fewer problems there are.

sections.title: Core Problems with Co-Located and Foreign-Agent Modes
sections.content:
In co-located mode, the mobile node gets an address at its current network and sets up an IPsec tunnel to the VPN gateway. It can then register with its home agent through the tunnel. However, the IPsec tunnel is identified by the mobile node's current IP address. Every time the mobile node moves to a new subnet and gets a new address, the tunnel must be re-established. This causes significant delays and packet loss in real-time applications like voice and video.

In foreign-agent mode, the situation is worse. The mobile node should contact a Foreign Agent (FA) at its current location, and the FA would relay registration requests to the Home Agent. But if the FA is outside the corporate network and the MIPv4 traffic is encrypted inside the IPsec tunnel, the FA cannot even read the MIPv4 registration messages to understand what it is relaying. Even if split tunneling allowed the mobile node to send clear-text registration requests to the FA, the FA would still not be able to deliver data packets back through the VPN gateway, because the gateway drops the IP-in-IP encapsulation that the FA uses.
sections.eli5: With co-located mode, every time you move to a new WiFi network, you have to reconnect to the VPN office tunnel, which takes seconds. With foreign agent mode, the office's security gateway can't even understand the mobile IP messages because they are encrypted.

sections.title: Requirements for a Working Solution
sections.content:
The document proposes ten solution guidelines. The solution must work with existing VPN gateways without firmware upgrades, must not require changes to IPsec or IKE standards, and must provide multi-vendor interoperability (MIPv4 agents, mobile clients, and VPN components from different vendors).

The solution must avoid or minimize IPsec tunnel SA (Security Association) renegotiation as the mobile node moves, to support fast handoffs. It must work with NAT gateways, must scale linearly with the number of mobile nodes, and must provide security equal to current nomadic remote access. It may introduce new MIPv4-compliant functional entities or additional header overhead if necessary.
sections.eli5: A real solution should work with VPN gateways that already exist, not require big changes to IPsec, and let different companies' products work together. It should also keep handoffs fast and security strong.

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Enterprises increasingly need to support mobile workers—employees on business trips, sales teams in the field, and remote branches. These workers need secure access to corporate resources and continuous session connectivity regardless of which network they are on. The demand for a working solution is driven by real operational needs, not academic interest.

The solution requires careful coordination between MIPv4 and IPsec behavior. Some proposals have involved running IPsec inside MIPv4 tunnels instead of the other way around, or introducing intermediate agents that understand both protocols. But all solutions must navigate the constraints outlined in the guidelines: existing infrastructure, multiple vendors, fast handoffs, and strong security.
sections.eli5: Many companies have mobile workers who need both strong security and continuous access, so someone has to solve this. The solution is not simple because it has to work with equipment that already exists.
